Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.

2611.27289.title: InterBand-EMG: A Cross-Band Foundation Model for Generalizable Hand-Pose Estimation
2611.27289.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables continuous hand-pose estimation, but learning representations that generalize across users and movements remains challenging. We introduce InterBand-EMG, which combines band-specific quantization with cross-band reconstruction and structured masked code prediction to learn transferable EMG representations for hand-pose tracking. We also introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose dataset comprising 1,227.74 hand-hours from 499 users across 68 movement categories. Experiments on emg2pose and SynapMyo show that InterBand-EMG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in joint-angle accuracy across all three generalization settings on both datasets. The source code and the SynapMyo dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

2611.27293.title: A Vision-Based Framework for Manual Assembly Verification and Adaptive Operator Assistance
2611.27293.abstract: Manual assembly remains difficult to monitor because operator actions, components, and task progress must be interpreted together. This paper presents a modular framework based on a single overhead red-green-blue (RGB) camera, combining object detection, hand-motion tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, task-specific pose classification, and configurable visual guidance. The system was evaluated during pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under three assistance conditions: full, mid, and no guidance. Mixed-effects analysis identified an association between assistance condition and a composite measure of motion quality, with lower estimated scores under mid and no guidance relative to full guidance. However, the condition-by-trial interaction was not statistically significant, and the estimated differences in learning trajectories remain descriptive. No condition differences were detected in completion time or failed-stage counts. The study demonstrates the integration of visual perception, procedural verification, and configurable operator feedback in a single-camera workflow. Selecting assistance according to operator expertise remains a design objective for future investigation.

2611.27302.title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
2611.27302.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

2611.27316.title: BioCL-POS: Biological Completer-aware Learning with Predictive Observation Selection - A Wild Ginseng Study
2611.27316.abstract: Growers and traders rely on root morphology to assess wild ginseng, yet breakage can obscure important structural traits. We study point cloud completion to provide geometric references for morphological analysis. Does providing more observed points always improve 3D completion? We test whether selected subsets improve recovery of the original missing region while keeping the pretrained completer fixed. We introduce BioCL-POS, an external selector that predicts how the completer responds to candidate inputs. For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. We use these spatial responses to estimate recovery quality and supervise them with measurements from actual completions. At inference, we select an input from the observed geometry and run the completer once. We evaluate four frozen completers on controlled gaps in ginseng and tree data at 5%,10%, and 20% omission, and examine 30% omission on ginseng. At 5--20% omission, we outperform full-input completion and all five alternative selectors on both datasets with all four completers. We achieve lower mean reconstruction error and higher mean F-score and coverage. We thus show that selecting observations can improve geometric recovery without retraining the completer, providing more accurate geometric references for subsequent morphological analysis.

2611.27340.title: CoGITAtion: Collaborative Gaze-based Interpretable Task-adaptive Representation for Privacy-sensitive Applications
2611.27340.abstract: Gaze-based analysis provides rich behavioural information for privacy-sensitive applications, but deployment is challenged by heterogeneous, scarce, and distributed data. We present CoGITAtion (Collaborative Gaze-based Interpretable Task-Adaptive Representation), a framework for privacy-preserving inference over vertically distributed gaze data. CoGITAtion transforms variable-length gaze recordings into compact, interpretable gaze-transition graphs and descriptors computed locally by each data owner. Task-adaptive models accommodate heterogeneous and missing feature blocks through task and availability gating, avoiding unnecessary private computation. Results show that shared components capture patterns that generalise across tasks, while task-specific components provide capacity without increasing model size. Public availability gating further reduces encrypted computation by removing branches determined by publicly known task and owner availability without altering predictions. Overall, CoGITAtion enables gaze model reuse, efficient privacy-preserving deployment, and robust inference under incomplete owner availability while retaining interpretable gaze representations.

2611.27341.title: ReSA: Preserving Reference-Specified Foreground in In-Context Segmentation
2611.27341.abstract: In-context segmentation uses annotated references to specify the target and its extent in a query image. Accurately transferring this reference-specified foreground requires recovering target regions while suppressing irrelevant predictions. We propose ReSA, a reference-guided framework that unifies query adaptation and mask selection through a shared reference kernel. ReSA leverages foreground and background reference prototypes to constrain prediction changes during adaptation and guide foreground selection through reference-weighted reconstruction. This shared guidance promotes consistent use of reference information across prediction refinement and mask formation. ReSA further selects among adapted predictions and aligns boundary refinement with the selected foreground threshold. We establish a theoretical bound connecting reference-response changes during adaptation and soft reconstruction. With a frozen visual encoder and lightweight test-time adaptation, ReSA requires no offline task training. Ablation studies demonstrate improved foreground retention and effective suppression of false-positive regions, while qualitative results show more complete masks with fewer isolated artifacts. Across ten object, part, and cross-domain segmentation benchmarks, ReSA achieves the highest average mIoU among the evaluated methods, reaching 62.6% in 1-shot and 71.8% in 5-shot.

2611.27352.title: PAVE: A Harness for Geometrically Consistent Road Network Modeling with Vision-Language Models
2611.27352.abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.

2611.27360.title: Borrow the Style, Follow the Prompt: Progressive Reference-Guided Stylization
2611.27360.abstract: Reference-guided text-to-image stylization transfers visual appearance to content specified by text, but the reference subjects and backgrounds can interfere with what the generated image depicts. Suppressing this unwanted information can also discard transferable texture and material cues, creating a tension between content control and faithful preservation of the reference style. Accordingly, we propose ProStyle, which learns a content-suppressed style prior through cross-content supervision on same-style pairs with different subjects and backgrounds and injects it with weak conditioning at auxiliary layers to strengthen style expression. Building on this prior, a complementary pathway learns residual corrections from full reference patch features with the content-suppressed style pathway frozen, before both pathways undergo joint refinement under the same objective. For cross-content learning and evaluation, we introduce ReConStyle, which provides 134K training pairs, two test settings, and object-level measures of target-content fidelity and reference-object overlap alongside style similarity and text alignment. ProStyle outperforms all compared SD1.5-based baselines and achieves the best average rank of 1.86 across four automatic and three human-evaluation criteria on ReConStyle-Full. In the user study, it substantially outperforms the baselines in text alignment and combined suitability, with selection rates of 84.36% and 50.90%, respectively. On the external Style-Rank benchmark, it also achieves the highest CLIP-Text and ImageReward scores.

2611.27381.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
2611.27381.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

2611.27389.title: Beyond What They Say: Cue Acknowledgment and Robustness in Vision-Language Models
2611.27389.abstract: Explanations are used to assess whether vision-language models rely on visual evidence or misleading suggestions. A response that explicitly names a cue can still follow it, making disclosure alone an incomplete basis for judging robustness. We ask whether greater cue acknowledgment accompanies greater resistance. We compare matched answers and explanations under helpful, misleading, and conflicting visual and textual cues while holding the underlying question and correct answer fixed. A paired comparison shows that a model can select the endorsed wrong answer more often while acknowledging the cues more often. Reduced silence therefore need not indicate improved resistance. Explanations may also mention a textual suggestion while omitting an accompanying visual cue. Requesting evidence and acknowledgment does not consistently improve resistance in the tested settings. Outcomes vary across models and settings, and these comparisons do not isolate a causal effect of acknowledgment. Evaluations should report cue following and acknowledgment on the same instances, distinguishing visual from textual cues.

2611.27407.title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
2611.27407.abstract: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.

2611.27412.title: Projector Time Map Calibration for Event-based Structured Light
2611.27412.abstract: Existing event-based structured light obtains a dense projector-camera correspondence from the timestamp of an event. It assumes that the projector scans a parallel raster and that the sensor timestamps each pixel independently, and we show that neither assumption holds. We obtain the correspondence from a temporal code that identifies the projector pixel directly and therefore needs no prior calibration, we calibrate the projector time map from the same recording, and we recover the geometry of the system and the offsets between its clocks by a spatio-temporal self-calibration in a preamble of a few seconds that needs no reference object and no second camera.

2611.27415.title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
2611.27415.abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.

2611.27453.title: AppCon-Bench: Perception and Misperception of Material Appearance in Vision-Language Models
2611.27453.abstract: Identifying the same material across changes in illumination or geometry is a critical ability for robust vision systems. Humans exhibit remarkable material appearance constancy, being able to recognize the intrinsic physical properties of an object's surface material across variations in extrinsic, confounding factors such as the lighting or the shape of such object. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate strong performance across a wide range of semantic vision tasks, yet their ability to interpret subtle mid-level perceptual attributes remains less understood. We introduce AppCon-Bench, a benchmark comprising five tasks designed to assess material appearance constancy under controlled variations in geometry and illumination, and evaluate representative VLMs alongside human observers, investigating their ability to maintain consistent material judgments across viewing conditions and experimental contexts. After thorough analysis, we identify several key findings that reveal both similarities and systematic differences between human and VLM material appearance perception, highlighting the value of evaluating perceptual successes and failures beyond overall accuracy and informing areas of improvement for current VLMs.

2611.27459.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
2611.27459.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.

2611.27465.title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
2611.27465.abstract: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.

2611.27469.title: PathOPEN: A pathologist-curated histopathology dataset for visual question answering
2611.27469.abstract: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.

2611.27501.title: Solar-Conditioned Flow Matching for Multitemporal Aerial Visible-to-Infrared Image Translation
2611.27501.abstract: Aerial visible-to-infrared (V2IR) image translation provides scalable thermal data across the full diurnal cycle. However, existing methods predominantly learn a static mapping within narrow acquisition windows. As the thermal state evolves throughout the day, a single visible image may correspond to multiple plausible IR appearances, making V2IR translation an inherently multitemporal task. This letter proposes solar-conditioned latent flow matching (Solar-Flow), which upgrades aerial V2IR translation from static mapping to multitemporal generation. First, we design three computable physical factors, namely the solar elevation, the thermal phase clock (TPC), and the flight altitude. The TPC counts the elapsed heating and cooling hours on a continuous 24-hour axis anchored at sunrise, so the thermal state stays well defined even at hours without training samples. Second, we inject the condition into every Transformer block of a pretrained flow matching generator through adaptive layer normalization. This design preserves translation fidelity and enables multitemporal generation. Finally, we construct a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering 14 hour groups. Solar-Flow achieves multitemporal generation on this dataset, where a single visible image is translated into plausible IR images at multiple times of day, even at hours that were never seen in training.

2611.27512.title: PGS-PCQA: Perceptually Gated Synthetic Supervision for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment
2611.27512.abstract: Existing no-reference point cloud quality assessment (NR-PCQA) methods perform well within individual datasets but generalize poorly across datasets. We identify insufficient distortion coverage in training data as a key cause: on unseen distortion types, models rank severity levels near chance or even in reverse. We propose perceptually gated synthetic supervision for no-reference point cloud quality assessment (PGS-PCQA), an NR-PCQA model trained with synthetic distortion ranking. It builds a synthetic distortion bank from source reference point clouds and uses within-type severity ranking as supervision in addition to the source mean opinion scores (MOS), requiring no subjective scores for the synthetic samples. Since higher severity does not always mean lower perceived quality, a perceptual gate softens the ranking targets of pairs with small perceptual differences in rendered views. The synthetic supervision is used only during training and needs no target-domain data. In a single training run on SJTU-PCQA, PGS-PCQA achieves Spearman rank correlation coefficients (SRCCs) of 0.709 on WPC and 0.751 on BASICS. The corresponding published DSP-PCQA scores are 0.595 and 0.723. Under reference-disjoint cross-validation, PGS-PCQA achieves SRCCs of 0.955 on SJTU-PCQA, 0.934 on WPC, 0.906 on BASICS, and 0.791 on LS-PCQA Part I. In the exclusion experiment, the reported scores for the reduced synthetic bank represent 58-65% of the full-bank SRCC gain relative to training without the bank. Code is available at this https URL.

2611.27515.title: Beyond a Single Human Demonstration: Learning from Scored Trajectory Alternatives for End-to-End Driving
2611.27515.abstract: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

2611.27517.title: EchoAlign: Echocardiography foundation model with multilevel report alignment
2611.27517.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.

2611.27521.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
2611.27521.abstract: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at this https URL.

2611.27529.title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
2611.27529.abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.

2611.27542.title: When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
2611.27542.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at this https URL.

2611.27585.title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
2611.27585.abstract: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above the best of nine imaging arms (0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, returns the same audit outcome from a different confounder. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

2611.27621.title: Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
2611.27621.abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

2611.27624.title: Points, Not Pixels: Keypoints, Masks and Oblique Geometry for Floating-Roof Tank Fill Estimation from Overhead Imagery
2611.27624.abstract: The floating roof of an oil storage tank rests on the stored liquid, so its depth below the rim measures how full the tank is. In optical overhead imagery, this depth appears only as the crescent shadow the rim casts on the roof, often a few pixels wide. Thin shadows are difficult to measure at overhead-image resolution, and nadir-based height conversions introduce errors in oblique views. Under a local affine camera, roof depth determines the rim-to-shadow displacement through the sun and camera geometry. We regress the boundaries as sub-pixel keypoints and invert this relation with a closed-form estimator that models oblique views. Available public tank datasets do not label roof position, so we introduce SynTank-25k, 24,987 physically based renders with exact roof, shadow and camera geometry. Using the oblique estimator, the keypoint pipeline reduces fill error by $22\%$ relative to the segmentation baseline on SynTank-25k. On shadows narrower than $6\text{ px}$, its error is also lower than that obtained by converting true binary masks. Our oblique estimator reduces the error of the nadir formula elevenfold at the steepest views. On 6,558 real NAIP tank crops defined by bounding boxes, about half of the fill estimates pass internal consistency checks; NAIP has no fill labels. Data and code will be released.

2611.27646.title: MoHA: Model-Conditioned Harness Adaptation for Long-Video Agents
2611.27646.abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at this https URL.

2611.27667.title: GeoScaffold: From Latent to Realized Geometry in Collaborative Detection
2611.27667.abstract: Most collaborative 3D detectors fuse bird's-eye-view (BEV) features from connected vehicles and roadside infrastructure to aggregate complementary observations. Although modern communication, alignment, and fusion pipelines encode rich latent geometry in the fused BEV features, the standard readout pipeline inherited from single-agent detectors, i.e., anchor scoring, box decoding, and non-maximum suppression (NMS), does not fully exploit these geometric cues. We empirically identify and quantify this gap on UrbanIng-V2X. Collaboration improves localization at about two-thirds of positive anchors, yet when NMS resolves two overlapping collaborative boxes of one object, it keeps the better-localized box less than half of the time. A key cause is a supervision mismatch: classification scores are trained only for foreground-background discrimination, so nothing in training requires them to rank boxes by localization quality. To address this limitation, we introduce GeoScaffold, a lightweight training-only auxiliary objective. It predicts a foreground mask at each positive anchor, i.e., the cells of a grid over the anchor that lie inside the ground-truth box, to supply the dense spatial supervision that the seven-dimensional box code leaves implicit. Its loss, added to the detection loss, updates the encoder and fusion modules through the fused BEV and trains the detector toward a better-localized box at every positive anchor, including the top-scored one. The auxiliary head is removed at inference, preserving the original detector architecture, communication logic, and inference cost. GeoScaffold raises AP@0.5 and AP@0.7 by 0.98 and 0.55 points on average across all 11 fusion methods on the UrbanIng-V2X validation split, with gains extending to most methods on an unseen intersection and to all ten methods that produce detections on V2V4Real.

2611.27674.title: CanopyFormer: Attention-Guided SegFormer for Explainable Forest Cover Segmentation
2611.27674.abstract: In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.

2611.27719.title: VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
2611.27719.abstract: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

2611.27728.title: Quantitative Measurement of Pavement Distress based on Vehicle Camera and Perspective Correction
2611.27728.abstract: Using image data is becoming an important method for highway agencies to automatically evaluate pavement conditions. However, most studies focus on improving detection accuracy rather than obtaining quantitative measurements, such as the length or area of pavement distress. Although field camera calibration can provide such measurements, it is impractical for large volumes of onboard images collected from different vehicles. This study develops a method to quantitatively measure pavement distress directly from in-vehicle camera images without on-site camera calibration. A quadrilateral region of interest is first identified based on lane detection and used to construct a perspective transformation matrix for image correction. Size correction is then performed using the proportions of road markings in the image and a specified scale, which also enables estimation of the actual width of the selected region. The corrected images are subsequently processed using object detection algorithms to obtain quantitative distress measurements. The proposed method can efficiently perform perspective correction for images collected by the same vehicle camera with minimal manual effort. The measured pavement patch lengths show a trend consistent with pavement friction data. By calibrating vehicle cameras using only image information, this study enables quantitative pavement distress detection without additional field experiments. The approach provides a practical solution for processing large volumes of vehicle-camera data, particularly as connected vehicles generate increasing amounts of uncalibrated roadway imagery.

2611.27756.title: Ref-YOLO-World: Decoupling Text-Side Computation for Efficient Referring Expression Comprehension on Edge Devices
2611.27756.abstract: Many high-accuracy referring expression comprehension (REC) methods produce image-dependent multimodal representations. These representations must be recomputed for every video frame, even when the referring expression remains unchanged. Fast open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World instead pre-encode text once and reuse it throughout the stream. However, encoding each referring expression as a single embedding prevents explicit token-level correspondence. We propose Ref-YOLO-World, which separates text-side computation that depends only on the referring expression from image processing and reuses its outputs across frames. Two lightweight modules inject cached per-token text features into YOLO-World's detection path. Ref-YOLO-World achieves 81.29% Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg val, the highest among REC models with a decoupled text branch, and consistently outperforms a fine-tuned YOLO-World. Precomputation reduces per-image inference time by 18.5%, yielding 47.0 FPS. A Core ML version runs at 15.73 FPS on an iPhone 15 Pro, demonstrating efficient on-device REC. Code is available at this https URL.

2611.27780.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
2611.27780.abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

2611.27788.title: When Does Looking Closer Pay Off? Simple Foveated ViTs for Fine-Grained Recognition
2611.27788.abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.

2611.27796.title: $\varepsilon$-SegFormer: Multi-Resolution Vision Transformers for Sparsely Supervised Segmentation in Electron Microscopy
2611.27796.abstract: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. We introduce $\varepsilon$-SegFormer, a multi-resolution Vision Transformer for sparsely supervised semantic segmentation, which builds on the architecture of MuViT and extends the training method of $\varepsilon$-Seg. For each labeled pixel, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer samples views at three physical resolutions centered on it, embeds their patches into a single token sequence, and encodes every token's position in image coordinates, so that attention relates all views in one shared frame. A segmentation head classifies the pixel from the tokens around it; during training, the pixel's own token is hidden, so the label must be predicted from context rather than local appearance. The model is trained in a single stage, without pretraining, with an auxiliary reconstruction loss. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer learns from about 10,000 labeled pixels among the 670 million voxels inside three cells, and, given the cell mask, segments nuclei, mitochondria and insulin granules in a slice of a fourth, unseen cell with an average Dice of 0.89 (0.91 after post-processing). Ablations show that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best, with the wider context entering through attention in the encoder.

2611.27854.title: DGC-Net: A Depth-Geometric Conditioning Network for Projection-Supervised OCTA Segmentation
2611.27854.abstract: OCTA segmentation is commonly formulated as a projection supervised task: models observe 3D volumetric scans but are supervised by 2D en-face semantic maps. Existing 2D and 3D-to-2D methods either discard axial information or compress depth responses into latent projections, leaving vessel crossings, diffuse capillary regions, and FAZ boundaries vulnerable to projection-induced ambiguity. We propose DGC-Net, a Depth-Geometric Conditioning Network that recasts 3D-to-2D OCTA segmentation as depth-geometrically conditioned prediction, where projected features are decoded with compact descriptors of axial vascular evidence. DGC-Net preserves local depth geometry through Depth-Moment Conditioning (DM), which injects axial localization and dispersion cues into the projection stream, and captures global depth layout through Holistic Depth-Geometry Modulation (HDM), which derives a raw-volume axial prior for final 2D decoding. Experiments on the OCTA-500 6mm and 3mm subsets show that DGC-Net achieves 83.58% and 88.62% mIoU, respectively, reaching state-of-the-art performance.

2611.27858.title: ENC-QA: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Vision-Language Models on Electronic Navigational Charts
2611.27858.abstract: Nautical charts encode safety-critical maritime information through standardized symbols, attributes, text, and heterogeneous geometries. Interpreting these charts and assessing the navigational significance of successive chart updates requires recognizing nautical features, determining their spatial relationships, and applying navigational knowledge. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising approach to nautical-chart interpretation, yet systematic evaluation of their fine-grained nautical feature recognition, chart-based spatial reasoning, and application of navigational knowledge to assessing chart changes remains limited. We introduce ENC-QA, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 77,312 questions derived from 6,612 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs). The benchmark evaluates four complementary capabilities: ENC Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Joint Perception and Spatial Reasoning, and Application. Of these, 8,227 questions form a progressive subset that decomposes selected chart-change cases into linked questions progressing from change detection to criticality assessment, enabling case-level analysis of how models use perceptual and spatial evidence to determine the navigational significance of chart changes. Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial limitations in fine-grained nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning. Controlled evidence interventions show that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy. Our findings establish ENC-QA as a diagnostic resource for nautical-chart understanding and safety-critical navigational decisions. We will release the benchmark and evaluation code upon publication.

2611.27876.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
2611.27876.abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at this https URL.

2611.27881.title: Interpretable Tissue Architecture Complements Pathology Foundation Models
2611.27881.abstract: Tissue architecture provides important information for histopathological assessment, yet its complementary predictive value alongside pathology foundation-model representations remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates whether interpretable measurements of cellular and multicellular tissue organization provide additional predictive information beyond learned representations. We introduce a 139-dimensional cellular-to-community representation comprising nine feature groups characterizing nuclear morphology, cellular composition, spatial connectivity, community organization, and cell-cell interactions. Their predictive contributions are systematically evaluated independently and through feature-level fusion with CTransPath and PLIP embeddings using multiple-instance learning (MIL). On the BCNB dataset, estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) classification is evaluated across four MIL architectures using five-fold patient-disjoint cross-validation. Selected CTransPath fusion configurations achieved mean ROC-AUC values of 0.9144 (ER) and 0.8360 (PR), while PLIP fusion achieved 0.8791 and 0.8015, respectively. Patient-level analyses identified ER-associated differences in nuclear morphology, graph connectivity, cellular communities, and cell-cell interactions. On LungHist700, selected fusion configurations achieved higher mean ROC-AUC across four classification tasks, including adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma (0.7967 versus 0.7137 for CTransPath alone). Overall, these findings suggest that interpretable tissue-architecture descriptors can complement foundation-model representations while providing measurable insights into histopathological organization.

2611.27901.title: QuantStream3D: Geometry-Aligned Low-Bit KV Cache Quantization for Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers
2611.27901.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.

2611.27905.title: AnimalFarm: Auditing the Generation and Detection of Hateful Images Featuring Anthropomorphic Characters
2611.27905.abstract: Anthropomorphic non-human characters have long been used to convey hateful messages targeting human groups, from Nazi-era propaganda to recent AI-generated imagery on social media. However, the safety risks posed by such imagery remain largely unexplored. We thus conduct the first systematic study of hateful image generation and detection involving anthropomorphic non-human characters. We construct a benchmark from conservatively screened source scenes, covering five character types and three image generation tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, and conversational image generation. Across 14,250 scheduled queries, image generation systems produce images for 92.1\% of queries, of which 95.9\% contain hateful content. We further collect 4,370 hateful images and evaluate five popular hateful-content detectors. Even the strongest detector, GPT-5.5, identifies only 73.9\% of hateful images, while most detect fewer than 58\%. Our analysis reveals that existing detectors often misclassify hateful images as benign when their main subjects are non-human characters. We explore two effective mitigation approaches: a training-free pipeline that maps non-human characters back to human representations before classification and a detector fine-tuned for this type of hateful content. These approaches achieve F1 scores of 0.962 and 0.979, respectively. Our findings expose significant safety gaps in both image generation and hateful-content detection. Disclaimer: This paper contains hateful text and imagery.

2611.27913.title: Star Panoptic Quality: Selectively Evaluating Split and Merged Instances
2611.27913.abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

2611.27931.title: DiTraR: Diverse Scorers and Transcript-Guided Re-ranking for Video Corpus Moment Retrieval
2611.27931.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval asks a system to find, in a large collection of untrimmed videos with subtitles, the video and the time interval that a natural-language query describes. We find that most top-ranked errors of a strong corpus-level scorer come from choosing the wrong video, not from imprecise boundaries, and that re-weighting the evidence the scorer already uses does not fix them. We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions. A witness-interval scorer decomposes the query into probes and scores every candidate interval of every corpus video exactly; a multi-scorer energy ensemble averages the energies of independently trained scorers before one exhaustive search; and a transcript verifier, a frozen language model that reads the time-stamped dialogue of the highest-ranked videos, re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries. With all settings frozen on development data and a single evaluation, DiTraR reaches 24.36 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on the TVR validation split. The ensemble improves queries about visual content, the verifier improves queries about dialogue, and their gains largely add up.

2611.26776.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
2611.26776.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

2611.26881.title: Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric
2611.26881.abstract: LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the generated answers fixed and vary only the Yes/No balance of the judge's few-shot examples across four demonstration sets. Each verdict is validated against a two-annotator human consensus on 200 examples per dataset. The judge's acceptance rate stays close to human consensus when its examples are balanced or skewed toward rejection, but jumps sharply (by about 30 points on NExT-QA and 20 on MSVD-QA, with a strongly one-sided error profile) when the examples are skewed toward acceptance; the opposite skew produces no matching drop. The bias is therefore one-directional within the tested range of label ratios. A separate five-draw analysis shows that results from a single example draw are unreliable, varying by up to 18 points, more than any difference between prompting conditions. We conclude that demonstration label bias in an LLM judge is a directional, inflation-only failure mode that can fabricate apparent benchmark gains but not losses, and that it is cheaply avoided by balancing the judge's examples and reporting results averaged over several draws.

2611.26907.title: A High-Compression Transformer VAE for Efficient and Controllable 3D Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Transformers
2611.26907.abstract: Many medical image processing tasks, such as completing missing regions or correcting acquisition artifacts, can be cast as volumetric generation conditioned on observations of the same patient. Diffusion Transformers offer scalable capacity and flexible conditioning for this setting, but they operate on a learned image representation that must preserve fine anatomical and pathological detail while keeping complete three-dimensional volumes tractable. We bring Transformer variational autoencoding and multimodal diffusion together to address this challenge. Trained on BrainTumor-256K, a 249M Transformer VAE encodes and decodes $256^3$ volumes 7.6x faster than a comparably sized CNN trained on the same collection. Their PSNR difference is near zero with training-sized crop inputs, but the Transformer leads by 0.749 dB with full-volume inputs and an unchanged scoring region. Increasing Transformer capacity to 499M improves PSNR across all four brain MRI evaluation sets while retaining 3.8x lower encoding-decoding latency than the CNN. Fast encoding also allows conditions to be constructed dynamically in image space during latent diffusion training. Within the compressed representation, a shared Diffusion Transformer integrates text and spatial references for volumetric synthesis, completion and restoration. The brain-trained autoencoder further transfers to non-brain MRI and CT without target-domain fine-tuning, extending its use beyond the anatomy and modality on which it was learned. The framework provides a reusable representation and conditioning interface for efficient, controllable medical image generation. Code is available at this https URL.

2611.26958.title: A Novel Dataset and Framework for Schenkerian Optical Music Recognition
2611.26958.abstract: Music theory enables performers, composers, and listeners to engage more deeply with music. Schenkerian analysis (SchA) is a particularly illustrative and widely used approach for modeling tonal structure, organizing music into hierarchical layers of harmonic and voice-leading relationships. Despite its importance in pedagogy and scholarship, producing well-formatted Schenkerian graphs remains difficult. A typical workflow might involve writing the Schenkerian analysis on paper, and then manually, painstakingly, entering each symbol by hand into music software, exporting to vector graphics, and manually refining layouts in graphical editors. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) systems for handwritten common western music notation (CWMN) can be leveraged for their ability to recognize small-scale symbols common to those in SchA. However, CWMN OMR models generally fail to recognize large symbols such as phrase slurs, struggle with dense notation, and do not recognize Schenkerian analysis markings. Thus, these models do not extend well to digitizing SchA. This paper introduces a novel framework for optical music recognition of both CWMN and SchA. Our novel contributions include (1) an ensemble model in which each individual model follows a different image-cropping scheme for improved object detection, (2) a topological neural network architecture for notation assembly, where candidate hyperedges attend to one another and perform hierarchical message passing, (3) the first dataset of labeled handwritten SchAs, gathered with novel model integration to the OMR-annotation software, MuNG Studio, and (4) the first algorithm for converting semantic Schenkerian graphs into typeset format.

2611.26971.title: RoboPRO: A Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-Aware Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
2611.26971.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: this https URL

2611.26978.title: Affine-Image Propagation for Tight and Scalable Neural Network Verification
2611.26978.abstract: While bound propagation methods are highly effective for certifying neural networks against $\ell_{\infty}$ adversaries, tight and scalable verification for $\ell_{2}$ adversaries remains a significant open challenge. Existing methods incur geometric loss by enclosing preactivation sets in elementwise intervals or axis-aligned ellipsoids, and functional loss by restricting the linear bounds constructed over those domains. Consequently, tight $\ell_{2}$ verification is currently restricted to Lipschitz-regularized networks where these approximations are accurate. In this paper, we introduce affine-image SDP-CROWN, a novel bound propagation method that better approximates preactivation domains using affine-image constraints and jointly optimizes the linear bound to adapt to the resulting domain. To bypass the prohibitive computational cost of dense semidefinite constraints required by the affine-image representation, we replace them with scaled diagonal-dominance conditions, allowing a GPU-accelerated implementation. Our method preserves the bound propagation recursion and can be integrated with branch-and-bound. On five MNIST and CIFAR-10 non-Lipschitz-regularized networks, our method improves verified accuracy over state-of-the-art methods by 17% to 57.5%. With branch-and-bound, these improvements increase to between 27% and 63.5%.

2611.26987.title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
2611.26987.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines.
