We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

2611.23197.title: Structure--Residual Inductive Biases for Language Model Pretraining
2611.23197.abstract: Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: this https URL

2611.23205.title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
2611.23205.abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

2611.23216.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
2611.23216.abstract: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

2611.23225.title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
2611.23225.abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at this https URL.

2611.23229.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
2611.23229.abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

2611.21771.title: An Open-Source da Vinci X/Xi Instrument Module for Laparoscopic Surgery Research
2611.21771.abstract: Studying electrosurgical tasks on a research robot requires control of both instrument motion and energy activation, along with a record of when each action occurs. This paper presents an open-source module for da Vinci X/Xi instruments on a UR5/UR5e robotic arm. Five motors transmit torque through timing belts to spring-loaded drive discs. An electrosurgical interposer accepts software commands, gives the surgeon's foot pedals priority, and records the source of each activation request. In bench testing, the interposer recorded all 12 activation and deactivation events from six pedal presses. Ex vivo demonstrations included monopolar and bipolar coagulation of splenic tissue and monopolar cutting during gallbladder dissection. Optical tracking of the Fenestrated Bipolar Forceps showed that calibration brought pitch and yaw gains from 0.904 and 1.14 to 1.00 and 1.02, respectively. The module enables researchers to record instrument motion, video, and the timing and source of electrosurgical commands during laparoscopic tasks.

2611.21783.title: Better Calibrated, Better Planned: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-ASV Informative Path Planning for Oil Spill Monitoring
2611.21783.abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.

2611.21789.title: ASTRA: ASV Simulator for Transferable Realistic Autonomy
2611.21789.abstract: Autonomy development for marine autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) remains challenging because field testing is costly and difficult to reproduce. Existing marine simulation tools provide mature capabilities in vessel dynamics, robotics integration, and visual rendering, but these strengths are emphasized differently across platforms. This paper presents ASTRA, an ASV simulation framework built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that combines marine vehicle dynamics, photorealistic perception, and Robot Operating System (ROS 2) autonomy interfaces within a common environment. ASTRA incorporates a Fossen-style marine dynamics model together with geometry-based buoyancy and programmable spectral wave disturbances, enabling non-planar hydrostatic and wave-induced motion. The simulator reproduces the sensor configuration of a physical BlueBoat testbed, including GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and RGB-D sensing exposed through ROS 2. This allows localization, perception, planning, and control software to be developed against interfaces consistent with the physical platform. The BlueBoat's existing ROS 2 localization and perception modules were ported directly into ASTRA, while targeted zero-propulsion experiments were used to verify the implemented wave-body coupling. The simulated roll response was consistent with the expected non-oscillatory hydrostatic behavior, and heave remained highly coherent with the generated wave field, with approximately unity gain at the dominant wave frequency in the tested sea states. ASTRA is intended as an open-source testbed for marine autonomy development, simulation-based benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.

2611.21806.title: A Probabilistic Lateral Motion Prediction Model with Improved Response Fidelity for Vehicle-in-the-Loop Simulation
2611.21806.abstract: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) simulation requires a lateral dynamics model that accurately reproduces vehicle responses and reliably generates horizontal lateral-position and heading commands through recursive integration. This paper presents a probabilistic lateral motion prediction model with improved response fidelity. A two-degree-of-freedom vehicle model provides the physical prior, while a recurrent neural network learns correlated residual corrections to lateral acceleration and yaw rate. To maintain prediction fidelity during recursive motion generation, multistep rollout training feeds corrected responses into subsequent states and histories and directly penalizes accumulated lateral-velocity error. A conditional Gaussian characterizes response uncertainty, which is propagated to lateral-response, position, and heading predictions through augmented-state linearization. Evaluation results demonstrate improved lateral-response and integrated-motion prediction. Compared with the Deep Dynamics lateral adaptation, the proposed model reduces mean lateral-position root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 0.596 m to 0.483 m, an improvement of 19.0%, while reducing mean lateral-velocity RMSE from 0.0469 m/s to 0.0441 m/s. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining physical priors, probabilistic residual learning, and multistep rollout training for response-faithful lateral motion prediction.

2611.21905.title: Agile Monoped Hopping on Complex and Discrete Terrain via Kinodynamic Planning with Distilled MPPI Steering
2611.21905.abstract: This paper presents FlowRRT, a kinodynamic planner for agile monoped hopping on discrete terrain. Steering for kinodynamic RRT on complex dynamical systems currently relies on motion primitives or closed-loop policies, limiting the diversity of motions or the planning speed. Distilling a trajectory optimizer avoids both, but existing methods regress a single solution per query, which fails on monoped hopping, where the feasible action set is narrow and disconnected. Our key insight is to treat steering as set-valued and predict the distribution of feasible actions instead. A multi-start MPPI expert collects the entire feasible set of each query offline, and conditional flow matching distills it into a generative sampler. With this sampler, FlowRRT coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and finds non-greedy maneuvers that are hard for reactive policies to discover. Benchmarks across different terrains show higher success rates and substantially shorter planning times than sampling-based baselines. On terrains with inclined platforms, FlowRRT reaches $80\%$ success within $1$~s, versus $24$~s for RL-RRT and $77$~s for SST. Sim-to-sim tracking in MuJoCo confirms accurate execution under full-order dynamics.

2611.21908.title: From Human Videos to Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Data: Confidence-Guided RL Refinement of Video Priors
2611.21908.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.

2611.22047.title: SE(3)-LIVOM: Adaptive Multi-LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry and Mapping
2611.22047.abstract: This paper presents SE(3)-LIVOM, the overall winner of the COMFORT Challenge at IROS 2026. The challenge asks for the trajectory of a legged robot in the GrandTour dataset, whose scenes include collapsed buildings, construction sites and snowfields. SE(3)-LIVOM runs in real time on two LiDARs, one camera and an IMU. Its frontend extends SE(3)-LIO to multiple LiDARs and a camera. Adaptive downsampling keeps the time per scan near 35 ms within and across scenes. An online backend corrects drift with a plane bundle adjustment over submaps and an incremental pose graph. With a single configuration for all scenes, the system reaches an average ATE of 1.40 cm on the six test scenes. The code is available at this https URL.

2611.22122.title: Low-speed Limit Cycle Walking of Planar X-shaped Bipedal Robot with Special Properties
2611.22122.abstract: This paper proposes a novel planar semicircular-footed X-shaped bipedal robot in which the center of mass of each leg link is at the same position as the hip joint, and discusses a method for generating a stable limit cycle gait on level ground. First, we outline the assumptions of the robot model with four degrees of freedom, and develop the mathematical equations of motion and collision. Second, we set the relative hip-joint angle as a control output and design a control system to follow it to the desired trajectory specified as a fifth-order function of time. Third, we mathematically show that there are special properties: the angular velocity of the swing leg does not change before and after the collision, and the time-integral of the control input becomes zero in a steady gait. We also mathematically show that the model has the feature that approximate linearization is effective and the antigravity effect of semicircular feet can be utilized. Through numerical simulations, we verify the validity of the theoretical results, and analyze some fundamental gait properties such as convergence speed and mechanical energy restoration.

2611.22146.title: HandUMI: A Modular Hand-Worn Parallel-Jaw Interface for Robot-Free Bimanual Data Capture
2611.22146.abstract: HandUMI captures robot-free bimanual demonstrations with a hand-worn parallel-jaw interface. Swappable fingertips match the robot's installed gripper; Quest/PICO controllers track hands and encoders measure aperture. Robot-agnostic recordings are retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms (median position error $\leq 1.2$ mm; $\leq 4.7$% of episodes rejected). On bimanual towel folding, 562 robot-free demonstrations train policies on real PiPER arms: ACT succeeds in 12/20 attempts and fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ in 7/20; ACT on the first 101 and base $\pi_{0.5}$ each succeed in 0/20. Hardware and software are open source (Apache-2.0), and a pair costs USD 557 with Quest 3S, excluding the optional ZED Mini and host computer. Project website: this https URL.

2611.22195.title: Haptic Probing for Subsurface-Aware Force Distribution on Layered Soft Tissue
2611.22195.abstract: Force-regulated contact with layered soft tissue fails most often where the subsurface composition changes: controllers infer the substrate from the loading signal alone, so the estimate guiding them lags the change---more acutely, we argue, over compliant than over bone-backed tissue. We remove that lag with a separate haptic channel. Under a light preload, a brief low-amplitude excitation lets the local dynamic admittance discriminate muscle from bone-backed tissue relative to a per-subject baseline, before task force is applied---active haptic sensing used to commit a control decision rather than to characterise tissue. A force- and tactile-driven distribution law then consumes that regime throughout execution: an instantaneous allocation equalises pressure across the engaged fingertips, while the regime sets the admissible pressure and hence the area the hand must recruit to deliver the target force---making patch area a controlled variable rather than a by-product. Probing, switches and recruitment are priced in a partitioned passivity budget, so safety monitoring cannot suppress the probe and a refused recruitment forfeits force tracking rather than the pressure bound. We report force tracking and pressure uniformity over curved, migrating contact on three human subjects, with regime labels from anatomical landmarks.

2611.22231.title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
2611.22231.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

2611.22258.title: ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
2611.22258.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.

2611.22302.title: Where Do Human-to-Robot Transfer Gains Come From?
2611.22302.abstract: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. In an HPT implementation on a 20-task MetaWorld suite with three training blocks, a constrained random 5,000-recording subset matches most of the task-informed subset's gain over the 40,000-recording pool at 20,000 updates (3.69 of 4.29 percentage points), leaving equal-size selection differences of 0.60 points at 5,000 recordings and 0.45 points at 1,250 recordings, with wide paired intervals. Across 12 comparisons, task orderings repeat across seeds for several contrasts, but a fixed predictor built from the other two seeds trails the mean or difficulty reference in at least one held-out fold for every comparison. Neither mechanism probe shows its predicted positive interaction: task-slot mismatch yields an interaction of $-0.0347$ points after adaptation, and in a six-task observation experiment the observation-by-pretraining interaction changes sign between seeds ($-18.29$ and $+1.04$ points) while full-state pretraining gains are positive in both ($+6.37$ and $+2.31$ points). This retrospective study shows how equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions change the interpretation of apparent transfer gains.

2611.22321.title: Beyond Episodic Recall: Experience-to-Knowledge Evolution for Lifelong Embodied Navigation
2611.22321.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.

2611.22356.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
2611.22356.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.

2611.22385.title: DGV-DLIVO: Degeneracy-Guided Visual Fusion for Direct LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry in Degenerate Tunnel Environments
2611.22385.abstract: Reliable localization in long underground infrastructures remains a major challenge for autonomous inspection robots. In hydropower spillway tunnels and drainage galleries, repetitive geometric structures provide insufficient constraints along the tunnel axis, while weak texture and illumination variations further degrade visual estimation. Under this coupled degradation, existing LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial odometry systems may lose the ability to recover continuous longitudinal motion. This paper presents DGV-DLIVO, a degeneracy-guided visual fusion for direct LiDAR-inertial-visual odometry for extreme tunnel environments. Instead of treating vision as a general complementary sensor, the proposed method exploits the LiDAR-degenerate direction as an active guidance signal to determine informative visual regions, establish LiDAR-anchored visual associations, and perform subspace-selective fusion. The visual constraints are introduced only into the deficient motion subspace, while unreliable LiDAR information in the same direction is adaptively suppressed and reliable geometric constraints are preserved. Real-world experiments in hydropower tunnels demonstrate that representative state-of-the-art LIO, LIVO, and VIO methods suffer from stagnation, oscillation, severe under-travel, curved drift, or divergence, whereas DGV-DLIVO maintains continuous and directionally consistent tunnel-axis motion estimation under both cart-mounted and handheld acquisition. It achieves a 91.4% progress ratio over the 40m tunnel sequence and significantly improves longitudinal recovery and trajectory stability. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of degeneracy-guided adaptive fusion for robotic inspection in severely degraded underground environments. The source code and a supplementary video are publicly available at this https URL.

2611.22388.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
2611.22388.abstract: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.

2611.22397.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
2611.22397.abstract: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues. In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.

2611.22445.title: Autonomous Track Racing with a Commercially Available Humanoid: System Design and Real-World Deployment
2611.22445.abstract: Learning-based methods now let humanoids run robustly, and they have begun to compete in athletic events. Yet few reports describe a complete autonomous humanoid running system in an actual race, where the robot must follow a lane at a new venue, pace itself within hardware limits, and finish without intervention. We report such a system deployed on the Unitree G1, a commercially available general-purpose humanoid, in the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events of the World Humanoid Robot Games 2026. The system integrates vision-based lane perception, path tracking, and a running policy trained by reinforcement learning with a human motion prior. To address the challenges of humanoid running, we stabilize head-camera images against body motion and use IMU-assisted leg odometry to bridge flight phases. To manage motor heating, we penalize hip-pitch torque during training, add heat-dissipation plates, and apply temperature-based speed limiting with event-specific pacing. The robot placed 13th of 74 in the 100 m, 10th of 44 in the 400 m first round before falling in the semifinal, and seventh of 35 in the 1500 m. In this deployment, thermal margin set the pace in every event, and the semifinal fall followed a lane-detection error.

2611.22447.title: COAST: Safe Flight Corridor Planner for Fast and Robust Snap Minimized Trajectories
2611.22447.abstract: Current B-Spline trajectory planners face a critical trade-off: they either sacrifice computational speed to maintain strict Safe Flight Corridor (SFC) guarantees, or they abandon hard safety bounds in favor of soft-constraint penalties to achieve real-time performance. We present COAST (Corridor-Optimized Aerially-Safe Trajectories), a B-Spline based, online trajectory planner capable of formulating snap minimized trajectories with SFC guarantees. COAST divides the problem into two stages: an A* based front-end that generates geometrically simple SFCs (represented as a chain of rectangular prisms), and a quadratic programming back-end for control point optimization. To handle the non-convexity of SFC intersections, we leverage the finite support property of B-Splines, to ensure the spline never exits SFC boundaries. The control point optimization incorporates MINVO transforms for kinodynamic bounding, allowing COAST to design non-conservative, dynamically feasible trajectories, while a snap minimization matrix calculation provides flight smoothness. This formulation provides a formal geometric containment guarantee, while ensuring mean trajectory computation times under 5 ms for real-time deployment. We validate our results through high-fidelity simulation experiments. The source code can be found at: this https URL

2611.22453.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
2611.22453.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

2611.22584.title: InteractVLA: Turning VLAs into Interactive Tools for Agentic Robotic Manipulation
2611.22584.abstract: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365. Project page: this https URL.

2611.22609.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
2611.22609.abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

2611.22625.title: VLM-guided Grounding Expert for Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension
2611.22625.abstract: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. Code will be released upon publication.

2611.22654.title: Risk Density RRT$^*$: Planning in the Space of Probability
2611.22654.abstract: Planning under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in robotics. While much of the literature seeks minimum-cost paths subject to probabilistic constraints, this paper instead considers collision probability, or risk classically defined as probability times severity, directly as the planning objective. We propose Risk Density RRT$^*$ (RD-RRT$^*$), an extension of RRT$^*$ for high-level planning in environments with deterministic and uncertain obstacles. RD-RRT$^*$ builds on Risk Density, a functional that evaluates a continuous path as a whole and provides a tractable approximation of its collision probability. The framework also supports severity-weighted risk and a hybrid variant that adds a path-length penalty, balancing risk and geometric efficiency while regularizing exploration in low-density regions. We validate the method across a wide range of scenarios. The results show that RD-RRT$^*$ consistently finds paths with lower estimated collision probability by optimizing a global risk-based objective. We further demonstrate the fidelity of the underlying approximation through Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we discuss how the topological structure induced by Risk Density may provide a useful representation of the environment and offer insights into risk-aware planning.

2611.22695.title: Learning Accurate End-Effector Trajectory Tracking with Inertial Feedback for a Quadruped Manipulator
2611.22695.abstract: Accurate end-effector trajectory tracking on quadruped manipulators is challenging because uncertainties in actuators, foot-ground contact, and geometric errors are propagated through the leg-arm kinematic chain. Detecting such errors requires sensing beyond joint encoders that can capture the effects of these uncertainties on the robot's motion, since joint encoders only provide measurements at the actuated joints and cannot fully observe mechanical errors such as backlash, dimensional inaccuracies, or structural deformation. This work addresses these challenges using a reinforcement learning framework with end-effector (EE) inertial feedback, targeting local high-accuracy manipulation while maintaining a nominal body pose and support configuration without intentional body motion or foot repositioning. The learned policy uses EE inertial measurements to compensate for tracking errors induced by uncertainties throughout the leg-arm system that cannot be fully inferred from proprioception alone. Simulation and real-world experiments on continuous EE trajectory tracking show overall improvements relative to nominal and proprioception-only baselines. In real-world experiments, the proposed policy reduces the MoCap-based RMSE by 17.3% and 28.0% relative to the nominal baseline under the two in-distribution (ID) command conditions, respectively, and by an additional 12.6% and 15.9% relative to the proprioception-only baseline. Furthermore, the trajectory-wise RMSE between FK-reconstructed and motion-capture-measured end-effector positions averaged 12.61+-2.15mm (mean+-standard deviation) across 24 controller-trajectory combinations, revealing a substantial discrepancy between nominal kinematic reconstruction and measured end-effector motion.

2611.22713.title: Body Schema Policy: Body as the Vision-Action Interface for Efficient Robot Loco-Manipulation
2611.22713.abstract: Currently, robots can learn whole-body loco-manipulation through scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet learn and act efficiently through a body schema that organizes what they see and how they move. We introduce Body Schema Policy (BSP), an imitation learning policy that builds such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the robot's kinematic tree, where learned screw motions carry features between links. Through body-queried vision, each body part retrieves its own visual evidence, which conditions the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, BSP returns an action chunk faster than any policy we compare. Compact, body-specific visual readouts also emerge without spatial supervision: manipulation commands depend strongly on task objects, while locomotion commands respond more broadly to the scene. On nine simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tasks, BSP matches the $\Psi_0$ humanoid foundation model with $75\times$ fewer parameters and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. The same holds on a real G1 and a Fetch mobile manipulator.

2611.22743.title: Stochastic Diversity Windows: Diagnosing Noise Influence in Robotic Diffusion Sampling
2611.22743.abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly adopted in robotics and control due to their capability to express multiple feasible solutions to a given task. However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.

2611.22767.title: Levio: Smart Actuated Back-Exoskeleton via Retrofit of a Commercial Passive Device
2611.22767.abstract: Passive back exoskeletons show promising benefits for reducing occupational musculoskeletal disorders. However, their assistance cannot be modulated towards the task requirements. Active exoskeletons offer opportunities for pose-specific assistance, but, developing these systems from scratch for research can be time consuming. Therefore, here, we present an accelerated design pipeline that retrofits a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) passive back exoskeleton, Laevo Flex, with COTS actuation (CubeMars AK10-9) and sensing (IMUs and load-cell) paradigms. Levio was able to provide assistance based on the user's pose. Nine participants performed stoop lifting with the original Laevo and the retrofit Levio system, in transparent and assisted modes. Compared to Laevo, Levio modulated the assistance provided between the bending and lifting phases of the stoop task. The passive assistance offered by Laevo was $25.2 \pm 4.3$ Nm and $30.6 \pm 9.5$ Nm respectively during the bending and lifting phases of the stoop tasks. Levio reduced the resistive torque during bending to $17.9 \pm 4.6$ Nm and offered increased assistance of $37.7 \pm 6.4$ Nm during lifting. Moreover, participants reported higher usability scores and lowest mean global discomfort score while using the Levio when compared to Laevo. These benefits demonstrates retrofitting passive exoskeletons is a viable direction for rapid prototyping of wearable exoskeletons for lifting.

2611.22797.title: Zero-Shot Compositional Generalization for Embodied Manipulation
2611.22797.abstract: Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, leaving many robot-skill combinations unobserved. Pooling these data shares visual knowledge, while joint labels remain tied to the demonstrating kinematic chain. We propose a geometry-supervised training framework for zero-shot composition of familiar robots and skills. The central insight is that a demonstrated command provides a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics supplies this supervision to foreign native action interfaces without their joint labels for that skill. Native reconstruction retains demonstrated configurations, and positive reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes through the target robot's native decoder. During policy learning, one prediction receives geometric supervision through both source and foreign native realizations. Matched supervision controls, repeated policy training and evaluations across three backbones and two simulators demonstrate improved transfer to missing robot-task combinations.

2611.22831.title: Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Balance on Dynamically Responsive Supports
2611.22831.abstract: Conventional balance formulations often assume a rigid, stationary support, decoupling body stabilization from support motion. This assumption becomes inadequate on mechanically responsive supports, creating a coupled control challenge: corrective body motions intended to restore equilibrium can also excite support motion. We formulate sustained balance as a coupled regulation problem that coordinates equilibrium restoration with suppression of motion induced by the robot's own corrections. We introduce LISST (Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Stabilization), a learning framework that accounts for how earlier actions shape the conditions for subsequent corrections. It uses recent observations to support immediate adjustments and longer histories to characterize persistent motion, with physical supervision relating the learned representation to robot-support behavior. To evaluate corrective actions, LISST uses coupled dynamics to assess both imbalance and the direction of motion. A Lyapunov-inspired criterion measures progress over finite windows, accommodating the transients required to restore balance. This physical evaluation guides joint-level policy learning through backpropagation through differentiable model rollouts. Privileged guidance focuses training on difficult states reached by the deployment policy and is transferred through distillation. The resulting policy operates using only onboard proprioception. Real-world experiments demonstrate that LISST maintains balance while limiting residual oscillations during continuous interaction with a dynamically responsive support. Video: this http URL.

2611.22850.title: Pelorus: Resource-Aware Lidar-Inertial Odometry
2611.22850.abstract: Lidar-inertial odometry (LIO) has an efficiency problem. High-resolution lidars produce millions of points per second that must be processed online on the resource-constrained hardware of robots, cars, or drones, yet most LIO methods neither bound their memory nor report their compute footprint. We introduce Pelorus, a resource-aware LIO with a fixed-capacity multiresolution map of voxelized normal distributions and an iterated equivariant state estimator. A relevance-based eviction keeps the map memory bounded, and a maturity-weighted map update suppresses inconsistent observations. The pipeline runs in parallel on CPUs and GPUs. On five sequences from three public datasets, Pelorus achieves the lowest relative pose error in seven of ten metrics with a small, bounded memory footprint and, with GPU offloading, the lowest CPU load of all compared methods. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, it processes a 128-beam lidar at 10 Hz. Pelorus is open source with CUDA, Vulkan, and Metal backends.

2611.22883.title: Fly as Instructed: Refining World-Action Policies for UAV Vision-Language Navigation
2611.22883.abstract: Natural language-guided UAV navigation enables intuitive human-robot interaction and flexible autonomous flight in complex environments. However, reliable navigation requires accurate instruction following, continuous task progress tracking, and safe obstacle avoidance, which remain challenging for existing world-action models that primarily focus on action prediction. To address these limitations, we propose a world-action learning framework that integrates three complementary mechanisms: a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion, recurrent instruction-consumption prediction to track task progress and determine termination, and Gaussian-scene post-training to enhance obstacle avoidance through trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback. Closed-loop evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate improvements in sequential task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination. Furthermore, direct one-step denoising reduces inference overhead, and real-world indoor and outdoor flights validate the framework's effectiveness.

2611.22908.title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
2611.22908.abstract: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. Arboreus has been open-sourced along with a dataset comprising 25 Boreal forest worlds of size 1000m2 corresponding to three real forest sites.

2611.22927.title: Sideslip-Conditioned Drift Trajectory Planning with Flow Matching and Control Barrier Functions
2611.22927.abstract: Drifting, the deliberate control of a vehicle at large sideslip angles, is relevant to both motorsport and recovery from unexpected oversteer. Existing autonomous drifting methods typically determine drift intensity through predefined reference trajectories, optimization objectives, or learned policy rewards, rather than accepting a desired sideslip angle as an explicit input. We propose, to the best of our knowledge, the first generative drift trajectory planner explicitly conditioned on a requested peak sideslip angle. A conditional flow matching model is trained on demonstrated drift laps with hindsight-derived sideslip labels and refined through reinforcement fine-tuning. A control barrier function (CBF) correction is then applied to satisfy model-based road, tire friction, and actuator constraints at the planning waypoints. In closed-loop experiments in the racing simulator Assetto Corsa, a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks the generated plans for six requested sideslip angles from 20 deg to 45 deg, with 30 laps (approximately 75 km) per request. The median peak sideslip angle measured across drift-corner passes follows the requested angle, with a mean absolute error of 1.2 deg across the six conditions. Ablation experiments show that reinforcement fine-tuning improves conditioning accuracy, while CBF correction substantially reduces off-road and spin events.

2611.22990.title: Physics-Informed Tactile-based Shape Estimation of Deformable Linear Objects
2611.22990.abstract: Accurate shape estimation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation, often hindered by visual occlusions and the high-dimensional configuration space of flexible materials. While Force/Torque (F/T) and vision-centric methods have been proposed, they frequently struggle with grasp-site ambiguities and environmental interference. In this letter, we investigate the hypothesis that global shape estimation can be achieved through tactile sensing and proprioception, without any visual perception. We contend that dense, high-resolution tactile imprints capture critical boundary conditions and contact gradients that are sufficient to resolve the high-dimensional configuration of the DLO. To prove this, we introduce a Physics-Informed Vision Transformer (ViT) framework that maps tactile images to a 3D vertex chain. By leveraging self-attention mechanisms and a physics-weighted loss function, our model enforces structural priors to ensure that the predicted geometry adheres to the object's physical manifold. Experimental results demonstrate that our tactile-based approach achieves superior reconstruction accuracy across Euclidean and Chamfer metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficiency of this modality, achieving model transfer to novel DLO materials and geometries. Our findings suggest that tactile feedback provides a robust and computationally efficient alternative for DLO state estimation in visually degraded or occluded environments.

2611.22994.title: Making Future-Predictive Representations Actionable
2611.22994.abstract: Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.

2611.23050.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
2611.23050.abstract: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at this https URL.

2611.23070.title: PAIR: Bringing Household Robots into the Smart Home
2611.23070.abstract: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{this https URL}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}

2611.23102.title: CADENCE: Learning Acyclic Gaits for Model-Based Quadruped Locomotion
2611.23102.abstract: Model-based quadruped controllers usually step on a cyclic gait, which lifts the legs in a fixed order on a fixed period, wherever the safe footholds are. We present CADENCE, a learned step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it picks one of at most 65 discrete choices: no step, or one leg's step to a safe foothold. It also predicts a swing time. We train CADENCE by reinforcement learning on top of a convex model predictive controller (MPC). Nothing prescribes a gait: there is no gait schedule, and the reward has no gait term, only a cost per step. The one structural constraint is that at most two legs may swing at once. The policy we analyzed developed an acyclic gait, with no fixed period or stepping order, yet it still paired diagonal legs. An inverse footstep model (IFM), fitted on a controller's logged steps, turns each foothold into a command. With only the IFM refitted, on fewer than 20,000 steps, CADENCE ran frozen on OCS2's nonlinear MPC. In simulated trials on a range of terrains (26% to 49% voids) and speeds (0.1 m/s and 0.2 m/s), it succeeded in 85.1% (mean of five seeds), against 67.8% for OCS2-Trot, 65.5% for OCS2-Single, and 39.6% in a static walk ablation of CADENCE. At 49% voids, it succeeded in 72.9%, against 43.0% for OCS2-Trot.

2611.23120.title: Pressure Drop: Gravity Vector Estimation from a Distributed Barometric Pressure Sensor Array
2611.23120.abstract: While gravity is often used in mobile robotics as a global constraint for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms, most estimation methods rely on indirect observation of the gravity vector. In this paper, we propose the use of altimeter measurements to directly observe the direction of the gravity vector. We provide a theoretical evaluation of the estimation noise and validate it through extensive experimental data, along with an evaluation of the impact of intersensor distance on our gravity vector estimates. Experimental results demonstrate that a median error of $0.87^\circ$ on the tilt estimation can be achieved with our system in semi-static scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this approach by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods based on Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs). We highlight that we achieve similar performance to that of IMU-based systems in highly dynamic scenarios and even outperform in specific cases of accelerometer measurement saturation. Finally, an additional experiment shows the potential use within a robotic system through the integration into an Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm.

2611.23149.title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
2611.23149.abstract: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

2611.23215.title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
2611.23215.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

2611.21795.title: The Impact of Scenario Representation in Scenario-based Optimization Certification
2611.21795.abstract: Scenario-based optimization provides finite-sample guarantees for decisions constructed from sampled uncertainty, but its certification procedures can be sensitive to how those samples are represented. We investigate this sensitivity under lossless scenario regrouping, which preserves the sampled information, feasible region, optimizer, and primitive violation probability. For an equal-allocation support-subsample certificate, we derive the distortion factor \(k^2(1-\epsilon)^{k-1}\), establish certification reversals between equivalent representations, and provide sufficient conditions for acceptance dominance under nested coarsening. We further apply nondegeneracy-free Wait-and-Judge theory to coordinatewise scenario envelopes, enabling stronger certification directly from the primitive observations. In paired scenario-MPC experiments, exact regrouping increases certification availability from 318 to 471 of 480 attempts without changing the samples, numerical proposals, or requiring any reduction in witness cardinality. Primitive Wait-and-Judge certification accepts the same 471 attempts without regrouping. These results demonstrate that apparent scenario sample-efficiency gains can arise from certificate accounting rather than additional information or reduced decision risk.

2611.22109.title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
2611.22109.abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.

2611.22399.title: Plenty to FRET About: From Hazard Analysis to Formal Requirements for Robot-Assisted Dressing
2611.22399.abstract: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.

2611.22403.title: BehaVerify: A Formal Verification Tool for Behavior Trees
2611.22403.abstract: This paper presents BehaVerify, a verification toolbox for behavior trees (BTs) and Neuro-Symbolic BTs. BTs are a graphical language for planning and sequencing behaviors - similar to extended state machines - and are increasingly used in safety-critical domains. BehaVerify enables users to specify a BT using a Domain Specific Language (DSL) with formal syntax and semantics. This language further includes Linear Temporal Logic and Computation Tree Logic specifications. BehaVerify uses an efficient encoding into nuXmv, called fastforwarding, to quickly verify if a specification holds over the BT. Additionally, BehaVerify can generate implementations of the BT in Python and Haskell. Through Python, BehaVerify has been integrated with PyTrees and Robot Operating System (ROS) and has been deployed to several autonomous robotic systems, including for verifying runtime monitors. While prior works have developed the underlying theory, this manuscript focuses on the toolbox usage, functionality and implementation. BehaVerify is open source: this https URL

2611.23021.title: Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Robust Synthesis of Signal Temporal Logic Specifications
2611.23021.abstract: Signal Temporal Logic is a popular framework for describing a robotic system's goals. Once described using a temporal logic framework, synthesis turns the goals into actual steps for the robots to follow. Currently, the state of the art for sound and complete synthesis is using Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), which struggles on long time horizons and large environments, preventing the construction of guaranteed safe plans for long deployments. This paper introduces a new synthesis method using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) which scales better for long deployments and adapts to environmental changes more quickly. We do this by introducing an encoding method for STL into SMT constraints, and an encoding method for discrete-time dynamical systems modeled as a transition system. We then conduct an empirical comparison of our SMT based methods against the state of the art MILP based methods. Results show that for this class of problems, SMT is an effective encoding strategy that performs the best on long time horizon tasks.

2611.23198.title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
